paras: The lynching of Jerry Taylor was the killing of a Black man in St. Helena Parish, Louisiana, on the night of November 22, 1888. He was accused of criminally assaulting the thirteen-year-old daughter of J. C. Williams. The case reached the press only as one-sentence wire and digest items, which ran in papers from Washington and New York to Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Dakota over the following week.

According to a telegraphic item in the Washington Evening Star of November 23, Taylor, "a negro," was lynched in St. Helena parish "last night" for criminally assaulting Williams's thirteen-year-old daughter. Weekly news digests dated the lynching "on the 22d" or "on Thursday" and described the charge more generally as "criminal assault on a young girl." None of the reports names a town, describes the people who killed him, says whether he had been arrested, or tells how he was killed.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The Evening Star placed its single unheadlined sentence among other short telegraphic items, between news of the Mexican cabinet and other national notes. The New York Evening World's news summary the same day reduced the case to a line about two Black men lynched, "one in Tennessee and the other in Louisiana, for assaulting white women," without naming either. Both papers gave the accusation as the reason for the killing and added no comment.

A syndicated weekly digest carried the same sentence, with Taylor identified as "(colored)," in the Mower County Transcript on November 28. On November 29 it appeared in the Iowa Plain Dealer, the Worthington Advance, the River Falls Journal, the Hand County Press and the Kanabec County Times, and on December 1 in the Chicago Citizen. In these columns the item sat between unrelated notes on executions, bank failures and accidents. No Louisiana paper's report was found, and the surviving coverage adds no detail beyond the first dispatch.

reader.title: Lynching of Jerry Taylor
bases: Every report says Jerry Taylor was 'lynched' over an accusation of assault on a girl (A1, A4); no other kind of violence is described.

The papers say Taylor was 'lynched' for an alleged criminal assault (A1, A4), which reports a killing outside the law under a pretext of punishing a crime; but no report describes the mob, its size or how he was killed, so a group of three or more is implied by the word only.

All reports are brief telegraphic or weekly-digest items, apparently from one dispatch (A1, A4 and its reprints A5-A10), with the unnamed Louisiana case in the Evening World summary (A2) consistent with it; no local or independent report was found.

framing.detail: The Evening Star ran a single unheadlined sentence among other telegraphic items, giving the accusation as the reason for the lynching.
The Evening World folded the case into a one-line summary of two lynchings 'for assaulting white women'.
Midwestern weeklies carried the same one-sentence digest item, Taylor identified as '(colored)', between unrelated news.
